chapter: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
title: Consultant to the Kennedy Center
summary: He suggested the Center should be the Palace of the world and attended meetings of its members.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: And when you were a consultant to the Kennedy Center, what did you do?

Well, the first -- see this is when the Center first opened, and about the most we did was try to get the Center -- how will I say that -- and when I first came there, the Center didn't seem to be -- have any particular object. It was going to be a terrific place in Washington, D.C.

And I, for one, in talking around to people -- I says well, I think you need another -- what was the theater in New York that everybody used to try to play -- Palace. I said this should be the Palace of the world. This is the greatest place, and they don't have a Palace in America any more. And that idea spread around and developed and everything, and it is. It's the greatest place in America to be showing now.

Just between members, you know, like they had hundreds -- they had a couple of hundred members. They'd have meetings every once in a while, and we even went up to -- I believe it was Hartford, or one of those towns, and

had meetings.

See, a lot of the people are big business people, and they have to pick out times when they -- most of them can attend. And the Center's a project for these people -- just a project of interest -- something to be interested in. And so now it has developed into a real terrific thing.
Did you make recommendations on music and types of music?

No. No, they seemed to take all types of music -- any music -- and present it. They have three theaters which can all operate at the same time. They have any number of restaurants. Oh, it's just a terrific complex there. Right across the street from Watergate.
